title: Supporting Family Without Going Broke: Helping Without Losing Yourself
description: School fees, medicine, rent, money sent home. How to help the people you love with a plan: a monthly number, a surprise pot, help that lasts, and kind ways to say not this time.

data.text: When your paycheck belongs to more people than you

In many families, the person with a steady income becomes the support. School fees for a sibling. Rent for a parent. A cousin's medicine. Money sent home every month. It comes from love and duty, and it matters.
It can also quietly drain you until you have nothing left, including for your own emergencies. This lesson isn't about helping less. It's about helping in a way you can keep doing.
The problem: support with no plan

data.title: Chidi's month
data.text: Chidi earns $1,500 a month. The requests arrive as they arrive: $200 for school fees, $120 for a relative's medicine, $80 for a funeral contribution, $50 “just this once”. This month he gives about $450, which is 30% of his income. Last month it was $620. He has no savings, and he paid his rent late twice. Chidi isn't failing at love. He's missing a plan.
Step 1: Decide the number before the asks arrive

Treat family support like a bill. Choose a monthly amount calmly, in advance, not in the middle of a phone call when you're feeling guilty. A common way is to choose a percentage of your income, such as 10% to 20%, then adjust for your situation.
Family support budget = income × the percentage you choose

data.title: A plan Chidi can live with
data.text: Chidi chooses 15% as regular support: $1,500 × 0.15 = $225. He adds a small surprise pot of 3%: $1,500 × 0.03 = $45. His monthly plan: must-pay bills $900, family support $225 + $45 = $270, savings $100, everything else $230. That adds up to $900 + $270 + $100 + $230 = $1,500.
Step 2: Build a surprise pot

Many requests are emergencies. If you plan for some of them, they stop being crises. Chidi's $45 a month becomes $45 × 12 = $540 a year for urgent help. When the pot is empty, it's empty, and that's a clear, kind reason to say “not this time”.
Step 3: Help in ways that last

Cash with no direction can vanish. Help that goes straight to the need, or helps someone earn, often does more. Pay the school fee directly to the school. Pay the pharmacy directly. Send food. Help with a CV, a job search or a skill.

data.title: Same money, different result
data.text: Every month Chidi sends his cousin $200 for “expenses”. Instead, he tries one purchase: a $400 sewing machine, the same as two months of support. The cousin starts earning $80 a month. After 3 months she has earned $80 × 3 = $240, and the requests can stop. Helping someone earn is support that shrinks the need.
Step 4: Say “not this time” kindly
You can say no without cutting anyone off. A few lines that work:
“I can't this month. I've reached what I planned for. Next month I can do $100.”
“I can't send cash, but I can pay the school fee directly.”
“Let's sit down together and see what the whole family can do.”

data.title: Limits protect the relationship
data.text: Giving beyond your means builds resentment, and resentment damages families. Clear, kind limits make it possible to keep helping.
Step 5: Talk about it as a family

In many families, relatives don't know your income, your rent or your costs. Share enough for them to understand your limits. Ask whether others can share the load. Agree who covers what, and rotate responsibilities where you can. One honest family conversation can replace dozens of last-minute requests.
What about loans to relatives?

Decide in advance whether you're lending or giving. If you lend to family, assume you may not see it again, and only lend what you could afford to lose. Never borrow money to lend it, and don't use your own emergency money for things that aren't emergencies.
Protect your own base first

If you lose your job or get sick, you can't support anyone. A small starter fund of your own is part of supporting your family, not a betrayal of them. Chidi's monthly must-pay costs are $900. Saving $100 a month, it would take $900 ÷ $100 = 9 months to build one month of cover. A slow start is still a start.

data.title: Set your number
data.text: Write your income, your must-pay bills, a regular support percentage and a surprise pot percentage. Check the total still leaves something for your own savings.

data.title: What to remember
points: Decide your family support number in advance, like a bill.
A percentage of income is an easy starting point, such as 10% to 20%.
A surprise pot turns emergencies into planned help.
Help that goes straight to the need, or helps someone earn, tends to last longer.
“Not this time” can be kind and clear.
Share enough with the family so they understand your limits.
Decide in advance whether a request is a loan or a gift.
Keep a small starter fund of your own.

data.text: The one thing to remember

data.title: A plan makes love sustainable
data.text: You can only help for years if you stay standing. A clear plan protects both you and the people who depend on you.

quiz.question: When is the best time to decide how much you'll give to family each month?
options: In advance, calmly, as part of your budget
After you've paid for everything else
quiz.explanation: Deciding in advance means the number is set by your plan, not by guilt in the moment.

quiz.question: Your income is $2,000 and you plan to give 15% to family. How much is that?
You put $45 a month into a surprise pot for family emergencies. How much is that after a year?
Setting a family support budget means you love your family less.
quiz.explanation: A plan lets you keep helping for the long term. Unplanned giving often ends in resentment or running out.

quiz.question: Which kind of help often lasts longer?
options: Paying a school fee directly or helping someone start earning
Giving more each time to make up for guilt
quiz.explanation: Help aimed at the need, or at helping someone earn, tends to shrink the need over time.

quiz.question: A relative asks for $300 and you've used up your planned amount. What's a kind, clear response?
options: “I can't this month, I've reached what I planned. I can help another way or next month.”
quiz.explanation: A kind, clear no, with another option, protects both the relationship and your plan.

quiz.question: Sharing enough about your costs with family helps them understand your limits.
quiz.explanation: When relatives understand your real costs, requests are more realistic and more spread out.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk of giving to family with no plan?
options: Your bank will close your account
You'll have nothing left for your own emergencies and may pay your own bills late
You'll receive too many thank-you notes
Your income will rise too quickly
quiz.explanation: Giving without limits can leave you with no safety net. That makes it harder to help anyone.
